I think more than that, I feel inspired by myself. I get full body goosebumps for myself

How can you make that your standard? Dancing to inspiring music really helps me connect to myself, I probably need to sleep more, and I think choosing that “I make more money and get to help more people” thing more often too instead of “it’s not working”

What happens that quietly pulls you out of that high-value cycle? You mentioned consuming, worrying, buffering. I think also I just feel beat down by life a little bit. Like it feels hard to manage taking care of myself, my business, my kid, my house. I guess it’s overwhelm.

At what point in your day do you switch from creating to consuming? Usually at naptime I consume more. Just because I’m overtired and parenting a toddler has been a lot for me. I love him dearly but it’s really hard sometimes. And I just want to turn off and feel better
answer:
Hi Coach,

You actually did such a good job laying this out, even if it felt hard while you were in it. What I notice most is you’re not lacking clarity on who that version of you is. You named her.

She’s the version of you who remembers you know things. Who trusts that even your “not best” is still valuable. Who feels taken care of, powerful, heard, and connected to yourself.

So instead of trying to figure out how to become her, I want to shift you slightly:

What’s pulling you out of her? And why?

Because from what you shared, it’s not confusion—it’s capacity. Life is full. You’re raising a toddler, running a business, taking care of a home. That’s not small. So when you drop into consuming, buffering, worrying… I don’t see a problem to fix. I see a human looking for relief.

And that matters, because relief isn’t wrong.
But where you go for it will either support you or slowly pull you out of that high-value cycle.

So I want to ask you this, and I’ll tell you why I’m asking:

When you hit that naptime moment and you go to consume what are you actually needing right then?

Not what you’re doing, but what you’re hoping to feel.

I’m asking because if we can get honest about the need (rest, quiet, space, being taken care of), then you can start meeting that need more intentionally in a way that still supports you.

Right now it sounds like it’s happening by default, not by decision.

And this ties into something you said that’s really important—you feel your best when you take care of yourself well.

So the question becomes:

How do you want to take care of yourself as the asset in your life and business, even inside a full life?

Not perfectly. But intentionally.

You also said something I don’t want to gloss over—your business did really well when you were in deep grief and didn’t have capacity.

That’s not ironic. That tells us something.

There was a version of you there who still believed: my brain is valuable, I have something to offer, even when things were hard.

So I want you to look at this:

What do you believe about yourself in hard moments that allows you to keep showing up?

I’m asking because that belief is what sustains you—not energy, not motivation.

And when that belief drops, everything feels heavier.

Same thing with selling.

Notice how when you’re in your best energy, you’re not “trying” to sell. You’re sharing, you’re connected, you’re inspired by yourself. That’s why it works.

So instead of making that the standard all the time, I’d look at it like this:

How quickly can I return to that version of me when I notice I’ve left it?

Because you will leave it. That’s part of the process. The goal isn’t to stay there it’s to move back faster.

Now let’s talk about overwhelm, because you named that too.

Overwhelm will keep things big, vague, and unsolved. It feels like “everything.”

So I want to offer you a shift:

The opposite of overwhelm isn’t feeling better it’s making a decision.

In those moments, instead of trying to fix the feeling, you can ask:

What am I choosing right now?

Am I choosing to consume and rest?
Or am I choosing to create?

And if it’s consuming can you choose it on purpose, without making it mean something has gone wrong?

That question matters because it puts you back in the driver’s seat. You’re not stuck you’re choosing.

And the more you practice that, the more you build trust with yourself.

Last thing I’ll say, because I hear this underneath everything you wrote You don’t need to push yourself into being some superhuman version of you to make this work.

You’re in entrepreneurship. You’re in motherhood. Life is full.

The work is learning how to support yourself inside of that, not override it.

So maybe the real question isn’t “how do I do more,” but:

Why do I want this? And what fuels me when I remember that?

Because you already have evidence you haven’t quit. You keep showing up.

That tells me there’s something here you already believe is possible.

Let’s build from that coach!

title: In person offers
question:
This past Saturday, I was at a women’s event and had 5 minutes to speak to the audience about grief and they offered half a table at the vendor area for all speakers. I now see how practicing my selling my offer matters. I added it to my talk and had a QR code for a Grief guide that 5 people subscribed to receive. At the vendor table I had business cards that had place to sign up for consultation.

I am reflecting back and questioning, why didn’t I make offers in person to those who came to my table after the talk?

My answer, because it felt awkward, presumptuous, direct – basically, my mind did not even go there out of fear. EEEKS. Fear of words getting all tumbled and confused. Fear of hearing some version of no…too my face.

What I will do differently. I will practice talking about my offer over and over again. I will create internal belief about my offer being exactly what my client needs and create urgency in me to act immediately with the belief that any of my client should not have to wait another day to feel better.

I have another talk coming up on Friday along with three leads from that event that I can follow up with and schedule to speak at their meeting/event.

Any other useful thoughts I missed?
answer:
Hey Coach!

Great work here! I don’t feel that much is missing but here is what I wanted to offer….

I see that you’re aware of the emotions you’re trying to avoid feeling. “Awkward. Presumptuous. Fear. Vulnerability. Rejection.”

You probably know this already, but just remember the goal isn’t necessarily to 
eliminate
 those emotions before making offers.

The goal is to become willing to feel them and make offers anyway. That is how we strengthen our self-leadership as entrepreneurs.

One of my favorite thoughts is: 
If there is nothing I’m unwilling to feel, there is nothing I’m unable to accomplish.
 What if success in this area isn’t about becoming someone who never feels awkward? What if it’s about becoming someone who is 
willing to feel awkward for 30 seconds
 in service of helping someone who may need what you offer?

Something else to consider:

What would the version of you who has already met her goals do at that vendor table?

The coach who has signed clients, filled her practice, and created the impact she desires?

Would she wait until she felt perfectly confident?

Or would she trust herself enough to extend the invitation and let the other person decide?

Last thing….

After Friday’s event, how are you going to take care of yourself for being brave? We spend so much time focusing on the outcome that we forget to celebrate the courage. Maybe it’s a walk, a favorite podcast, dinner with a friend, a bubble bath, or simply acknowledging yourself for taking risks. The more you teach your nervous system that being visible, making offers, and hearing “no” are safe experiences to have, the easier this process becomes. You’ve got this coach! Amazing work!

title: amount of work as a teacher and coach
question:
Dear coaches,

you have helped me so much with answering my last questions. Thank you!

Today I have another question:

I am building my coaching business, I have 5 clients right now and I am still working 18 hours as a teacher besides that.

My plan was to lower my hours working as a teacher so that I have more time taking on more clients.

Now I heard Stacey say in a podcast episode, that she didn’t lower her work at Walmart for a long time and that in the beginning when her business was still a ‘baby’, she didn’t use it to pay her personal bills.

If I go down from 18 to 14 lessons working as a teacher, I would have to rely more on the coaching income because I would have trouble paying all my bills only from the teacher salary and probably I would feel more stressed if one month I didn’t get new clients. Now my idea is to stick to those 18 hours and build my capacity to take on more clients or schedule some clients in the late afternoon where I don’t have school lessons. Right now I have Wednesdays off and I’m coaching a lot then.

I have a family and a dog, so I really need a certain income.

One more thing: I see myself improving in coaching, I don’t need so much time preparing the coaching sessions anymore and that will help to taking on more clients an still work 18 hours at school, I guess.

Am I missing some thougts? What do you think?

Thank you so much in advance.

Best wishes from Germany, Alexandra
answer:
Hey coach,

This is such a great question let’s explore it together. I want to start by pointing out something really important that you’re already doing, you’re noticing the compound effect of building momentum and increasing your capacity. You’re coaching 5 clients, preparing less, and getting more efficient. That matters! Celebrate that and highlight it.  That’s evidence your capacity is already growing.

It’s important your brain sees this. What you’re doing right now is becoming your new normal. And every time you stretch your capacity, you expand it.

So I want to offer you a question here, because it helps uncover what you believe you’re capable of:
What if you think your capacity is at an 8 or 9… but it’s actually at a 2?
How would you think differently about what you can handle if you believed this is just the beginning for you?

Because the way you’re thinking about your capacity will either open things up or quietly cap you.

Another piece I want you to look at is how you’re talking to yourself about your life, teaching, coaching, family, your dog, all of it. That internal dialogue matters more than the schedule itself.

So notice this:
When you feel like you’re hitting your limit, what are you thinking? Why? 
And when you feel energized and capable, what are you thinking?  Why?

What you believe in those moments are not true or false they are optional.

I’m asking because this is where your energy is actually coming from, not just your circumstances, but your thoughts about them. Those thought feeling combos either fuel you or drain you.

Now, about the example you shared, what Stacey did was continue working while building her business, in part because it reduced pressure. When your income isn’t dependent on coaching yet, selling can feel cleaner, less urgent, less heavy.

So a useful question here is:
How do you feel about adding pressure to your coaching income right now?
Do you notice that creating more urgency feels motivating… or does it feel stressful and tight?

There’s no right answer but there is awareness in that answer.

And zooming out a bit there are people with families, responsibilities, full schedules who are building businesses. So it’s worth asking:
What do you think they believe that allows them to do that?
How are they thinking about their capacity, their time, their responsibility?

Not to compare but to borrow beliefs that might serve you.

At the end of the day, this isn’t about finding the “right” way. You can reduce your teaching hours, or you can keep them as they are. Both paths work.

The real question is:
Do you like your reasons for the choice you’re making?
And do those reasons create more trust in yourself or more pressure?

I don’t think you’re missing anything Coach,  I think your brain is just trying to find the right answer when really, this is a decision you get to make and back yourself in. What do you want to do?  That will always be the best choice.

What are your thoughts?

title: moving into selling courses 3
question:
Hi! Thank you so much! It’s so interesting my brain does not want to take this deeper lol it’s just uncomfortable!

C: Selling courses

T: I can reach more people with less of my time and make more money doing it.

F: Excited

A: talk about my offers, think about what people need to hear, feel good about what I know and how I can help – and doing it easily and fluidly. When I’m really in this energy a post can take me 5 minutes. Sometimes I get an idea while I’m driving and then create it once I park. It feels simple, easy doable. I’m actually not spending much time – and usually I’m not sitting down at my desk to do it. I feel easily inspired so it’s not a problem to post – ideas flow. I also take action on my ideas easily, I’m not waffling with “should I share this?” I just see it’s valuable and share it. Mostly I just live my life and have ideas and do them quickly. I’m thinking ooo that’s a good idea. Yes, that’s valuable. Oh this is something I say all the time, here I’ll share it. Or even this is what I’m learning or thinking, I bet one person will resonate with this. I’m just being someone who can help and who does.

R: get myself out there more aka creating value, which is what leads to reaching more people and making more money. That matters, because it shifts this from “trying to sell” into “showing up to serve”

C: Selling courses

T: It’s not working. I don’t know how to sell this.

F: Defeated

A: cry, want to hide, feel graspy, spend time wishing my circumstances would change, do everything besides work in my business, spend a lot of time scrolling or learning stuff that I already know (thinking I need to listen to a podcast or Stacey or another mentor or telling myself I should buy xyz to help me with my business), I feel bad, I spend time worrying about the future – what if I don’t figure this out? I numb with food, tv, instagram, I’m not as kind to my spouse or kid, I don’t respond to my personal texts as quickly, life in general feels hard, I don’t do the house tasks like laundry either, it feels hard to even take care of myself – like I put off showering or making lunch, spend time worrying about things that take up space but don’t matter when I’m in the other energy

R: $0 – also keeping you from learning how to sell, from gathering data, from adjusting, from getting better.

I want to create one course sale a day. More would be amazing but it’s okay to start here.
answer:
Hey coach,

First, this is such important awareness. The moment you noticed your brain didn’t want to go deeper? Of course it didn’t. Your brain is wired to conserve energy and avoid discomfort. It’s not a problem it’s protection. This is where you become emotionally stronger, getting yourself to do things you don’t feel like doing.  That is what everyone wants to get masterful at doing. Great job!

You moved through that anyway, you moved through resistance, friction, discomfort that is how you stay in the intentional model.

That matters more than the exercise itself, because this is exactly what your clients experience. “I just couldn’t get myself to do it.” Now you don’t just understand that, you’ve lived it. That’s where your power as a coach comes from. So don’t skip past that win. Let your brain register: this effort was worth it. What worked well is you working the process.

Now let’s actually use what you wrote, because there’s a lot of gold here.

When I read your intentional model, I’m less focused on the actions right now and more interested in who you are being when you’re in that thinking.

T- “I can reach more people with less of my time and make more money.”

That thought creates an entirely different identity. You’re not trying to sell, you’re someone who naturally shares value. You’re available to ideas. You trust them. You move quickly. There’s no drama about posting, no overthinking.

So the real question becomes,  how do you relate to that version of you? How do you strengthen that identity?

Not “how do I sell more,” but:

What allows that version of me to exist more often? Why? Get specific to deepen the who before how.  When you become that version the creativity the how reveals itself simple and doable.

Now let’s look at the other side.

In your unintentional model, you said: “It’s not working. I don’t know how to sell this.”

When you think that thought, what are you making it mean about you? I’m asking because that’s the moment everything shifts. It’s usually not just “this isn’t working.” It quietly becomes:

“Maybe I can’t do this.”

“Maybe I’m not good at this.”

“Maybe this won’t work for me.”

And from there, your actions make perfect sense. You’re not avoiding your business you’re responding to what feels like failure.

That’s why you’re consuming, scrolling, buffering. Not because you lack discipline, but because those actions soften the discomfort just enough to keep you from fully feeling it and from taking more action. Those actions dull the intense negative emotions and when you feel low you are less likely to go out and share.  You can clearly see that model is you now working the process.

So instead of trying to “fix” the actions, I want to go one layer deeper.

What do you need to believe in that moment to keep showing up? Not at a 10/10 belief. Just enough to stay in motion.

You’ve already proven that in your intentional model. You don’t sit around convincing yourself, you move, and the belief follows. So what would it look like to rely less on feeling fully confident, and more on staying in the process?

For example:

What if the goal isn’t just  “one sale a day” right now but “clean selling actions a day”?

I’m offering that because your current goal is only result-based, and your brain might start using the lack of that result as evidence that it’s not working pulling you right back into that defeated cycle.

But if you shift to:

“I’m someone who sells every day, regardless of the result,” Now you’re back in identity.

What does selling actually look like for you when you’re in your best energy? Keep that top of mind when you approach your day.  Not the pressured, graspy version but the version you described:

sharing ideas, speaking to one person, offering value naturally.

How can you make that your standard?

What happens  that quietly pulls you out of that high-value cycle? You mentioned consuming, worrying, buffering.

At what point in your day do you switch from creating to consuming?That moment matters, because that’s where the shift happens. If you can catch it there, you can redirect it. This isn’t about doing more. It’s about staying with the version of you who already knows how to do this.

You’ve already built the roadmap. Now it’s about practicing staying on it. Ok coach, this is really good work.

title: I need to see if I can afford it
question:
People say in my consults – I need to see if I can afford it – do the numbers.

And it seems like that might be a place I could dig in with them – and unearth some objections – but I’ve struggled to know what to say.

I say something like, ‘oh what do you need to look at’

And they say, ‘oh if I can afford it.’

And then I dont know where to go after that.

Should I close the conversation there – or is there something I could say to open up more thinking?
answer:
Yes – you want to open up the conversation if they are open to doing that.

How you do that is by you getting curious. You want to get to know them and their mind and how they are thinking and feeling.  It’s not about getting a yes – it’s about creating that safe space for them to really think through this decision. They signed up for the consult with you for a reason.

When you are asking “Oh what do you need to look at?” now, what are you thinking and feeling in that moment? We want to check in to see if there is some thoughts or feelings coming up that are blocking you from knowing what to say next.

When they say “Oh if I can afford it.” – you can get curious about that. You don’t need to follow a script here, but think about what you might ask me if you were coaching me on deciding if I should sign up for a gym membership or not. What might you ask me if I said I wasn’t sure if I could afford it?

It could be something like this:

“Yah, you don’t want to sign up for the gym membership if it’s going to cause more stress due to finances. Do you think you could afford it and there are maybe some other hesitations coming up about going? Or is it really just the money?”

Or maybe “You know you keep thinking about signing up for a gym membership. What do you think would happen if you did decide to do it and spend $___/month? and then, What do you think would happen 3 months from now if you didn’t do it?”

The goal is to create a safe, open space for them to explore with you. Let’s put this into practice now. If you had to re-do the last consult where this came up, what might you have said or asked?

And – are you setting up a follow up call? If someone truly does need to look at their budget, etc, that’s okay. You can set up a follow up call with them so there are clear next steps for them to take. That gives them a chance to do whatever they need to do and still circle back with you so they can ask any questions they might have or have support from you in figuring out their final decision.

title: Consult evaluations -please tell me what you see!
question:
WW did a very thorough intake and spotted her gap immediately – she’s not making offers at all and she hasn’t had sales calls in a while. She is increasing her networking and how she’s meeting people and has an excellent offer that she feels great about but is holding back from inviting people in. I felt very connected and calm, clear and present with her. I was listening deeply. I think I explained the bridging the gap really well and she agreed this was going to be the thing that would make a huge difference in her business. She wants to do the work but said ‘that price is way out of my budget’

WDW – when she said ‘that price is way out of my budget’ and also ‘I can’t justify paying that out when I don’t have an income’ I didn’t ask more questions about it, just took that as the circumstance.

WDD – ask more questions! Stay with her brain when she says the words ‘I can’t justify paying that when I don’t have an income’ instead of agreeing. What would it look like if she did want to pay for it? Would she need the business to generate that investment back right away to afford continuing to work together? Does she have the money or access to the money now but feels fear about investing it? So many questions I could have asked.

I’m struggling a bit with all my consults when it comes down to the very last piece – helping them with objections. My instinct is that I have to sink into more compassion and understanding FOR them so I can be calmer and clearer and ask the ‘awkward’ question. I’d love your take on it please!
answer:
You know you want to sink into compassion and understanding for them. When she had that objection about price – what were your thoughts and feelings in that moment? We want to look at what’s happening now so we know what needs to shift to get into compassion and understanding.

When someone says they can’t afford it – it might be that they really can’t. That can be true. It can also be true that they could afford it, but it’s scary. They might worry it won’t work. They feel bad spending money on themselves. etc. Millions of things. What we want to do is get curious. We want to help them fully understand why they are saying that. Is it that they really can’t afford it? Or is it some other hesitation? You already know there are so many questions you could have asked to help you better understand her and what was happening.

Let’s look at your thoughts about your price too. Is it a price your clients could typically afford? Why or why not? When we are clear about our thoughts on the price it helps us show up and get curious about what’s happening for a client instead of being in our own thoughts about the price.

question:
Yes, I do see this. And reading it back reflects to me makes it very clear that the common thread isn’t strategy or consistency, it’s how fully I’m embodying leadership while I’m executing.

Here’s how I’m thinking about the how and the shift.

Helpful thoughts to anchor into (instead of engagement = proof)
